findings.headline: Transformation programme delivering savings heavily weighted to cost avoidance rather than structural budget cuts
findings.detail: The £4.08m transformation benefit delivered in 2025-26 comprised only £113,593 in actual base budget savings (2.8%) and £3.967m in cost avoidance or overspend reduction (97.2%). Future years show similar pattern: £511,074 base budget savings forecast for 2026-27 but £5.896m cost avoidance. This suggests the council is not yet achieving structural cost reductions.
findings.matters: Cost avoidance is temporary and demand-dependent; structural base budget savings are permanent. A lender should distinguish between the two when assessing the council's progress toward addressing the medium-term budget gap.
findings.figures: 2025-26: £113,593 base budget savings + £3.967m cost avoidance = £4.08m total; 2026-27 forecast: £511,074 base budget savings + £5.896m cost avoidance; 2027-28 forecast: £1.032m base budget savings + £8.924m cost avoidance
findings.quote: Continued Transformation Board oversight of delivery of the council's transformation programme and associated financial benefits, with £4.08m delivered in 2025/26 against forecast categories within the programme, comprising £113,593 of base budget savings delivered and £3.967m of cost avoidance / overspend reduction delivered.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will create a new South East Essex Council from April 2028; council is alert to resource diversion risk impacting service delivery
findings.detail: Following government approval in March 2026, the council will merge with Castle Point, Rochford and Essex County Council services to form a new unitary authority from 1 April 2028. The council recognises 'there is a significant amount of work and resource required to deliver the transition, and the Council is alert to the risk that the diversion of resources required to deliver these changes impacts on the ongoing delivery of services to residents and other stakeholders,' requiring ongoing management and potential adjustment of priorities.
findings.matters: A major structural change creates a multi-year demand on management attention and resources at a time of budget pressure; a lender should understand how this affects transformation delivery and financial discipline during transition.
findings.figures: Implementation date 1 April 2028; no resource estimates given
findings.quote: There is a significant amount of work and resource required to deliver the transition, and the Council is alert to the risk that the diversion of resources required to deliver these changes impacts on the ongoing delivery of services to residents and other stakeholders.

findings.headline: Data Protection Act compliance failure: council did not meet timescales for processing Subject Access Requests in 2025-26
findings.detail: Subject Access Request (SAR) volumes increased 33% year-on-year to 281 requests, and 'although during 2025/26 the council did not meet its obligations to process all requests within the timescales prescribed by the Data Protection Act, compliance has further improved,' reaching 60.55% on-time compliance (up from 44%). This is an explicit breach of statutory duty.
findings.matters: A lender should be aware of regulatory breaches and governance weaknesses; data protection failures can carry fines and reputational damage. The council is below statutory requirements.
findings.figures: 281 SARs received (33% increase on prior year); 60.55% on-time compliance (target is 100% within statutory timescale); improvement noted but still non-compliant
findings.quote: Although during 2025/26 the council did not meet its obligations to process all requests within the timescales prescribed by the Data Protection Act, compliance has further improved.

findings.headline: Housing regulator issued C3 serious failings rating for safety and quality compliance; council working through required improvements
findings.detail: The Regulator for Social Housing inspected the council's housing management services in April 2025 and issued a C3 grading in September 2025, indicating 'serious failings in the housing management service at the time of the inspection, particularly relating to safety and quality compliance.' The council has committed to working closely with the regulator to deliver improvements, but timescale and scope of required investment are not detailed.
findings.matters: A serious regulator finding suggests governance and control failures in a material service; a lender needs to understand the cost of remediation and whether it will compete with other budget pressures.
findings.figures: C3 rating (serious failings); improvements noted at time of publication; action plan due March 2027
findings.quote: The outcome of the inspection was published in September 2025, with a grading of C3 awarded, indicating there were serious failings in the housing management service at the time of the inspection, particularly relating to safety and quality compliance.

findings.headline: Better Queensway regeneration partnership with Swan Housing collapsed; scheme is in reprogramming with uncertain completion timeline
findings.detail: The council's long-term joint venture partnership (Porters Place LLP) with Swan BQ to deliver the Better Queensway central Southend regeneration ended when Sanctuary Housing (who acquired Swan) chose to step away from the partnership. The council has brought Southend Housing Ltd into the partnership to maintain legal compliance, but is now 'engaging with the market to inform the reprogramming of the regeneration scheme' with no confirmed route to market stated.
findings.matters: A major regeneration capital scheme has lost its private sector partner and timeline certainty; a lender should understand any financial exposure, whether the council is carrying reputational or financial loss, and whether the scheme remains affordable.
findings.figures: No financial figures given; 'initial highways aspects' completed during 2024-25; route to market expected to be confirmed during 2026-27
findings.quote: Unfortunately, following a period of due diligence by Sanctuary Housing, they decided to focus on managing their new and existing tenants and on developments which were already on-site. They therefore declared that they wished to step away from Better Queensway and the partnership with the council.

findings.headline: Children's services placement costs required intensive leader-led intervention and fortnightly review to tackle budget pressures
findings.detail: The council ran regular focus sessions chaired by the Leader of the Council and fortnightly placement review meetings chaired by a chief officer specifically to manage children's residential and high-cost supported accommodation placement costs. The document indicates this was a significant budget pressure requiring this level of governance attention throughout the year, later extended to adult social care and homelessness.
findings.matters: A lender should understand the scale and trajectory of these placement cost pressures, as they directly impact budget sustainability and whether the measures taken have successfully stabilised demand.
findings.figures: No specific figures given; measures extended to adult social care in Q4 2025-26
findings.quote: Throughout 2025/26 there was intensive monitoring and oversight of children's residential and high cost supported accommodation placements to tackle placement budget pressures... All placements were regularly reviewed throughout the year to ensure the children we care for receive the right support at the right price.

findings.headline: Capital borrowing programme cut by £7m, reducing financing costs by £0.5m for 2026-27
findings.detail: The council reduced its capital investment programme from £95m (with £27m borrowing) at the start of 2025-26 to £65m (with £20m borrowing) by February 2026, following challenge sessions. This reduction in borrowing is presented as prudent, though the reason for the cut and whether it signals affordability pressure is not explained.
findings.matters: A significant unplanned reduction in the capital programme mid-year may indicate cash flow or affordability constraints, and a lender should understand whether this is planned prudence or financial necessity.
findings.figures: £95m to £65m programme reduction; borrowing reduced from £27m to £20m (£7m reduction); financing cost benefit of £0.5m for 2026-27
findings.quote: At the start of the 2025/26 financial year, the council had a capital investment programme budget of £95million, £27million of which was financed by borrowing. Following capital challenge sessions this was reduced to £65million at February 2026, £20million of which was financed by borrowing.

findings.headline: Revenues team capacity constraints prevented completion of historical Council Tax debt review, identifying only £400k of £13M overdue debt as irrecoverable
findings.detail: The council planned a full review of £13.0M in legacy Council Tax arrears but could not complete it. Onboarding 7 new officers requiring training and 2 vacant posts under recruitment reduced capacity. Only £2.6M was collected (against £3.2M target) and £400k of irrecoverable debt identified. Work continues into 2026/27.
findings.matters: An incomplete debt review means the council's bad debt provision may not accurately reflect recoverable debt, and staffing gaps risk material bad debts going unidentified and ultimately reducing available revenue.
findings.figures: Historical debt opening balance £13.0M; £2.6M collected (vs £3.2M target); £400k written off; 7 new officers onboarded; 2 positions vacant
findings.quote: Capacity constraints were the primary limiting factor, with the onboarding of 7 new officers within the Revenues Services team, who all required significant training and structured support. In addition, two vacant posts, currently under recruitment, have further reduced the team's resource.

findings.headline: Fraud investigation in Adult Services with £0.5M debt awaiting criminal prosecution scheduled for June 2026
findings.detail: A single case under investigation by the Council's Fraud Team has resulted in £0.500M of additional debt being raised. The case is awaiting court hearing for prosecution in June 2026, creating governance and internal control risk.
findings.matters: Fraud within a financial services area erodes the reliability of the council's debt reporting and internal controls, and a material single-case fraud raises questions about control effectiveness elsewhere.
findings.figures: £0.500M debt from single fraud case; court hearing scheduled June 2026
findings.quote: There is also a single specific case being investigated by the Fraud Team which has raised an additional £0.500M of debt. This is currently awaiting Court hearing for prosecution that is scheduled for June 2026.

findings.headline: Adult Services debt of £4.9M overdue over one year and charged to service users' estates carries explicit unsecured recovery risk
findings.detail: Of £8.655M total Adult Services debt outstanding, £4.875M (57%) has been overdue for more than one year and is mostly charged directly to service users' estates. The paper explicitly identifies this as 'a significant risk to recovery as it is unsecured'. Only temporary additional resource has been allocated to address this.
findings.matters: Unsecured personal debts outstanding for years against individuals with limited means represent material write-off risk and constrain the council's ability to fund statutory services or service borrowing commitments.
findings.figures: £4.875M unsecured debt overdue >1 year out of £8.655M total Adult Services debt; decrease of only £0.145M year-on-year despite £2.4M new debt raised
findings.quote: Of the remaining £4.875M (57%), the majority has been overdue for greater than one year and in some cases, the customer ID reflects that the debt is now charged to the service users' estate. This poses a significant risk to recovery as it is unsecured.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Annual Treasury Management report - Cabinet - 15 June 2026
findings.headline: £21.4m property fund investment faces uncertain merger-or-termination vote on 18 June 2026
findings.detail: Patrizia Hanover Property Unit Trust, in which the council holds £21.38m, is exploring a merger with another property fund. An EGM on 6 March approved merger negotiations. A second EGM is scheduled for 18 June 2026 to vote on proceeding with merger on 30 June; if that fails, unitholders vote on terminating the trust. Outcome is uncertain and creates near-term volatility.
findings.matters: A material 29% of the council's investment portfolio faces liquidation or merger risk; either outcome carries costs (exit fees, forced sale of properties, merger restructuring) and locks up capital for transition.
findings.figures: £21.380m held in Patrizia fund (of £73.303m total investments)
findings.quote: there is currently another Extraordinary General Meeting planned for 18 June, for the unitholders to vote on the merger going ahead on 30 June. If that resolution does not pass, unitholders will vote on the termination of the Trust.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Annual Treasury Management report - Cabinet - 15 June 2026
findings.headline: Financing costs ratio increased to 10.69%, above the revised budget of 10.37%
findings.detail: The proportion of the general fund's revenue budget consumed by borrowing costs increased from the budgeted 10.37% to 10.69% in actual outturn, indicating cost pressure from the existing debt portfolio.
findings.matters: Increasing financing costs as a share of revenue budget reduce funds available for service delivery and indicate growing cost pressure from existing debt.
findings.figures: 10.69% actual vs 10.37% revised budget; General Fund financing costs
findings.quote: the actual figure in 2025/26 was 10.69%, which is slightly higher than the revised budget in 2025/26 of 10.37%.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Annual Treasury Management report - Cabinet - 15 June 2026
findings.headline: No new PWLB borrowing taken; council deliberately keeping cash low to avoid new borrowing requirement
findings.detail: The council took no new external PWLB loans in 2025/26 and kept investment balances lower than budgeted to delay when borrowing would become necessary. Investment income was £0.711m below budget because of this deliberately constrained cash position, despite having £58m+ of capital to fund.
findings.matters: Shows the council managing its financial position by deferring both capital investment and new borrowing, indicating a tighter position than headline prudential indicators suggest.
findings.figures: Investment income £4.246m vs budget £4.957m; average in-house balances £62.4m vs £79.1m prior year; no new PWLB loans drawn
findings.quote: This was due to there being less in-house balances to invest as the Council seeks to delay borrowing for as long as possible.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Annual Treasury Management report - Cabinet - 15 June 2026
findings.headline: Capital expenditure deferred following capital challenge sessions; £7m underspend
findings.detail: The council's capital programme was cut by £7m (revised budget £65.164m vs actual £58.161m) mainly because schemes were deferred following 'capital challenge sessions'. The underspend was led by borrowing-funded schemes. This indicates the council is managing capital investment against financial constraints.
findings.matters: Deferred capital spending signals financial tightness and the council's priorities in managing available resources; lenders need to understand capital investment cycles and capacity.
findings.figures: Total capital expenditure variance (7.003)m; borrowing-financed spending variance (4.428)m against revised budget
findings.quote: This is mainly due to schemes which have been deferred to later years following the capital challenge sessions led by the Cabinet Member for Finance and Transport.

findings.headline: Children Looked After placement costs and budget pressure mounting
findings.detail: Demand for CLA placements is outstripping supply nationally and locally. The council is increasingly using expensive Independent Fostering Agencies rather than in-house carers. Placement complexity is rising, requiring more specialist support and creating increased costs and pressure on the placement budget.
findings.matters: CLA placements are a high-cost, demand-driven service; rising costs without corresponding savings elsewhere worsen the council's financial sustainability problem.
findings.figures: Residual risk impact 4, likelihood 2, score 8. Target score 4.
findings.quote: Increased costs and pressure on the placement budget.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation vesting 1st April 2028 creating concurrent capacity crisis
findings.detail: The council is merging into a new South East Essex Council on 1st April 2028. Senior managers are being drawn into multiple concurrent workstreams (LGR, transformation, business-as-usual) alongside hard deadlines. The register flags risk that delivery of business-as-usual and statutory/core services could be impacted by over-commitment of staff.
findings.matters: Service delivery failures during reorganisation would create operational risk; the confluence of LGR, transformation demands, and financial pressure creates a cascading failure scenario.
findings.figures: Residual risk impact 3, likelihood 3, score 9. Target score 3.
findings.quote: Failure in the councils readiness for vesting day of the new South East Essex Council (1st April 2028). Same senior managers being drawn into multiple concurrent workstreams alongside business as usual.

findings.headline: Local plan submission deadline at 31 December 2026 with significant consequences if missed
findings.detail: Failure to submit the local plan by 31 December 2026 under current regulations would force a restart under new regulations, causing significantly delayed adoption. Consequences include reduced control over land allocation, reduced development funding opportunities, and risk of government intervention.
findings.matters: A missed planning deadline undermines the council's ability to direct economic development and attract investment; it also signals governance weakness to lenders.
findings.figures: Residual risk impact 2, likelihood 3, score 6. Target score 4.
findings.quote: Failure to submit local plan by 31 December 2026 under the current regulations leading to significantly delayed adoption of a local plan due to need to restart under new regulations.

findings.headline: Expenditure exceeds available resources and reserves cannot sustain the gap
findings.detail: The council explicitly acknowledges its expenditure continues to exceed the level of resources available. Reserves are being used unsustainably to bridge income and expenditure gaps in the medium term. The S151 Officer is flagged as potentially having to issue a S114 report to Full Council, and external auditors may issue a qualified opinion. Government could step in to administer council functions.
findings.matters: A S114 notice or government intervention is a material credit event; unsustainable reserve use signals a council approaching insolvency.
findings.figures: Residual risk impact 4, likelihood 3, score 12. Target risk score unchanged at 12 (no improvement trajectory identified).
findings.quote: Use of the Council's reserves is not sustainable to bridge income / expenditure funding gaps in the medium term. The S151 Officer has to issue a S114 report to Full Council. External auditor issues a qualified opinion report. Government may step in to administer Council functions.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and capital outturn report - 2025-26 - 15 June Cabinet
findings.headline: The council faces preparation for Local Government Reorganisation by April 2028 alongside ongoing structural financial deficits, requiring simultaneous transformation and merger integration.
findings.detail: Multiple references indicate the council is preparing for LGR, including developing a 5UA Model business case. This adds significant organisational disruption and cost during a period when the council is already consuming reserves due to demand-led overspends. The timing compounds financial risk: transformation programmes may slip, integration costs are unknowable, and senior management attention is divided.
findings.matters: LGR creates sovereign uncertainty for a council already in financial stress. Lenders need to understand how LGR may affect borrowing, covenant compliance, and service continuity, plus what the actual integration costs will be.
findings.figures: £0.2M of the Local Government Reform / Devolution Reserve used in 2025/26 for business case development and implementation staffing.
findings.quote: Change is being driven by a combination of external and internal factors, with a broad and significant range of possible regional and local scenarios likely to unfold.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and capital outturn report - 2025-26 - 15 June Cabinet
findings.headline: Adult Social Care saw a £0.8M income loss from client contributions and care package income below forecast, signalling either policy changes or demand for lower-cost services.
findings.detail: Income from client contributions to care packages fell by £0.8M vs. forecast at Period 8. The report notes several financial assessments resulted in lower contribution levels, and homecare income was lower than planned. This may reflect both policy decisions (contribution reductions) and actual caseload shift toward lower-value services, indicating either changing demographics or demand management.
findings.matters: Revenue from service users is a material income stream; a shortfall suggests either council policy (setting lower contributions) or market shift (fewer high-cost placements) that affects budget assumptions.
findings.figures: £0.8M reduction in income from client contributions vs. forecast.
findings.quote: There has been a reduction in income from client contributions towards individual care packages of £0.8M compared to the forecast at Period 8.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and capital outturn report - 2025-26 - 15 June Cabinet
findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only 89.3% of budget (£58.161M vs £65.164M), with significant shortfalls in housing acquisition, new build and regeneration schemes.
findings.detail: Council Housing New Build delivered only 22.0% of budget; Housing Acquisitions 63.0%; Enterprise and Regeneration 84.1%. These underperformances signal either delivery constraints (resource, land, planning), market conditions, or prioritisation changes. The HRA planned capital spend (RCCO) had to be reduced from £7.237M to £1.365M mid-year, suggesting housing ambitions could not be achieved.
findings.matters: Slippage in housing development programmes affects long-term regeneration strategy and income assumptions. Repeated shortfalls suggest systemic delivery challenges or unrealistic planning rather than one-off slippage.
findings.figures: Council Housing New Build: £1.771M budget, £0.390M spent (22.0%); Housing Acquisitions: £1.727M budget, £1.088M spent (63.0%); HRA revenue contribution to capital reduced from £7.237M to £1.365M.
findings.quote: It has not been possible to deliver the elements of the capital investment programme funded by RCCO which included housing acquisitions and delivering new housing construction projects.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and capital outturn report - 2025-26 - 15 June Cabinet
findings.headline: The new waste collection contract has revealed workforce cost variances and operational mismatches creating immediate pressures of £0.66M (provision) and £0.2M on sack collection services.
findings.detail: The workforce transfer from the previous contractor created a £0.66M provision for unresolved cost variances on staffing numbers and pay rates still under negotiation. Additionally, the wheeled bin suitability criteria used to design the service specification did not match actual property types on audit, creating an extra £0.2M cost in 2025/26. These suggest procurement assumptions were not validated before contract go-live.
findings.matters: Large contracts with long-term cost exposure (waste is multi-year) need accurate specification and workforce planning. Unresolved disputes and underspends on capital (bins) create future budget uncertainty.
findings.figures: £0.66M provision for workforce cost reconciliation pending negotiations; £0.2M additional cost pressure for actual sack collection properties vs. forecast; £2.9M wheeled bin capital spend during the year.
findings.quote: As a result, the operational requirements of the service differ from those anticipated when the contract was procured, creating an additional cost pressure of £0.2M in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and capital outturn report - 2025-26 - 15 June Cabinet
findings.headline: Direct Payments provider Vibrance went into administration in November 2025, creating £1.26M of emergency additional cost in Adult Social Care alone.
findings.detail: The failure was sudden and required immediate remedial spending to ensure continuity of care for vulnerable residents receiving social care through this provider. An additional £0.18M was incurred in Children's Services as well. This was an exceptional and unforecasted cost pressure that the council could not avoid, illustrating exposure to external provider failure in commissioned services.
findings.matters: Provider failure in outsourced social care creates unbudgeted, unavoidable costs and service continuity risk. This reveals dependency on single providers and lack of redundancy in commissioned care arrangements, a governance and operational risk.
findings.figures: £1.26M additional cost in Adult Social Care; £0.18M in Children's; total £1.44M from provider failure.
findings.quote: Following the administration of the Direct Payment provider (Vibrance) in November 2025, the Council has incurred additional costs of £1.26M across Adult Social Care to ensure continuity of care and support for these vulnerable residents. This represented an exceptional cost pressure arising from the failure of a key external provider, with immediate action required to maintain essential services and protect those affected.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and capital outturn report - 2025-26 - 15 June Cabinet
findings.headline: The council drew £24M from earmarked reserves to fund 2025/26 spending, reversing years of prudent reserve-building and signalling unsustainable cost structures.
findings.detail: The £24M reserve drawdown was used to absorb exceptional demand and cost pressures that could not be controlled within the approved budget. While the council states these reserves were intentionally established to manage known risks, the scale of drawdown (against a gross spend of ~£187M) signals the reserves function as a pressure valve rather than an occasional buffer. The council is now rebuilding specific social care risk reserves for 2026/27, implying expectation of further overspends.
findings.matters: Reliance on reserves to fund structural deficits is a one-off solution and erodes financial flexibility. Lenders assess reserve adequacy and sustainability; this drawdown rate cannot be sustained indefinitely.
findings.figures: £24M total appropriation from earmarked reserves 2025/26; opening reserves £59.395M, closing reserves £35.348M (40% reduction); planned replenishment of Adults social care risk reserve to £1.0M and Children's to £2.5M for 2026/27.
findings.quote: The combination of pressures described in paragraphs 4.1 to 4.6 resulted in the use of £24M of the Council's earmarked reserves during the period from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and capital outturn report - 2025-26 - 15 June Cabinet
findings.headline: Children's social care placement costs spiralled despite £4M of targeted interventions, driving the majority of the council's £12.0M overspend.
findings.detail: Demand for high-cost residential and specialist residential placements continued to grow sharply. An additional 15 placements were required at average cost ~£0.38M each, which alone drove £2.8M of the increase from the forecast position. Despite focused challenge and redesign work delivered £4M of cost avoidance, it was insufficient to contain overall demand growth. Children's Services accounted for £11.6M of the £12.0M net overspend (97% of total).
findings.matters: This reveals a demand problem that formal interventions and oversight cannot contain at current price and care model, suggesting structural pressures that will persist into future years regardless of management action.
findings.figures: £11.6M overspend in Children's Learning and SEND; £17.1M overspend across Children's and Adult Social Care combined (143% of overall net overspend); 15 additional placements at ~£0.38M each; £4M of cost avoidance delivered but still insufficient.
findings.quote: An additional 15 placements were required, at an average full-year cost of approximately £0.38M each, this was the major contributing factor behind the additional £2.8M increase in overspending reported at the financial year end.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3(ii) - General Fund Budget Savings and Income Generation 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Prior-year EV charging savings revised down by 50%, from £90K to £45K
findings.detail: A savings initiative from the 2024/25 budget cycle (IGC-10, EV charging points and commission income) has been adjusted in the current plan, with the estimated annual benefit cut from £90K to £45K. The 'updated assessment' provides no explanation for the scale of the revision.
findings.matters: This demonstrates that prior budget estimates were not achieved as planned. For a lender reviewing whether the council can deliver its current £6.1M savings target, evidence that previous estimates were 50% optimistic raises credibility questions about all proposed savings, particularly income-dependent ones.
findings.figures: £90K original estimate → £45K revised (50% reduction)
findings.quote: An updated assessment has reduced the full year effect to £45,000 (down from £90,000). [EDEP]

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3(ii) - General Fund Budget Savings and Income Generation 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Major Transformation Programme delivering £750K savings has no finalised staffing impact plan
findings.detail: The Transformation Programme covering Third Party spend, Zero Based Budgeting, Activity Analysis, One Council redesign, Data Transformation, Estates, Children's Services Commissioning, My Southend, and Business World shows 'TBD' for FTE staffing implications, indicating the delivery plan is not yet finalised. This programme contributes £750K to the 2026-27 savings target.
findings.matters: A £750K annual saving without a finalised implementation plan raises delivery confidence risk. This represents 12% of the total savings package, and the lack of clarity on staffing implications suggests the council has committed to a savings target before fully designing how to achieve it.
findings.figures: £750K per year; FTE impact TBD
findings.quote: The 2026/27 programme includes projects on Third Party spend, Zero Based Budgeting and Activity Analysis as well as the continuation of the One Council (service redesign), Data Transformation, Estates, Children's Services Commissioning, My Southend (resident access) and Business World (internal corporate systems) projects. [X-Council: EDSC] TBD

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3(ii) - General Fund Budget Savings and Income Generation 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Fees and charges income expected to increase five-fold from £250K to £1.25M by 2028-29
findings.detail: The council projects fees and charges yield of £250K in 2026/27, rising to £750K in 2027/28 and £1.25M in 2028/29. The document describes this as 'MTFP assumed increase in yield from fees and charges' with no breakdown by service area or explanation of the mechanism driving such rapid growth.
findings.matters: A 400% increase in fees income over three years is material to the budget and suggests either major service expansion, significant price rises, or volume growth. Lenders need assurance this is realistic, as fees income is often more volatile and demand-dependent than budget projections assume.
findings.quote: Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP) assumed increase in yield from fees and charges. [X-Council]

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3(ii) - General Fund Budget Savings and Income Generation 2026-27 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Adult Social Care client contributions expected to rise 214% over three years, from £260K to £815K
findings.detail: The council expects Adult Social Care income from service users to grow from £260K in 2026/27 to £535K in 2027/28 and £815K in 2028/29. The paper states these increases are 'directly related to the rise in cost of delivery' but provides no detail on whether this reflects rising unit costs, increased placements, or policy change. The escalation continues beyond the forecast period.
findings.matters: Such rapid escalation in client contributions signals either rising complexity and cost of Adult Social Care or a material shift in how the service is funded. For a lender, this suggests the council expects sustained cost growth in a statutory service with limited discretion, which creates budget risk if contributions cannot be fully collected or sustained.
findings.quote: Expected increase in client contributions which is directly related to the rise in cost of delivery. [EDAC]

findings.headline: High risk that some savings proposals will not deliver or services will exceed investment allowances in 2026/27
findings.detail: The S151 Officer explicitly acknowledges 'the high risk surrounding the non-delivery of some of the savings proposals or services exceeding investment and pressure proposals within the budget package for 2026/27.' This is identified as an exceptional risk.
findings.matters: Unachieved savings targets force mid-year cuts or reserve drawdowns; non-delivery indicates the budget plan is not fully owned or achievable.
findings.figures: Savings risk identified for 2026/27 budget package; no specific amounts quantified
findings.quote: The high risk surrounding the non-delivery of some of the savings proposals or services exceeding investment and pressure proposals within the budget package for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivery and phasing is uncertain despite challenge sessions; many projects still lack viable business cases
findings.detail: The General Fund Capital Budget is described as 'substantial' but 'what is less certain...is the actual phasing of expenditure, which urgently needs further consideration and further prioritisation.' Many new projects are 'still subject to a viable business case,' implying decision-making is incomplete.
findings.matters: Capital project slippage or overspend indicates programme management weakness and can delay critical service improvements or infrastructure replacement.
findings.figures: General Fund Capital Budget is substantial; specific size not quantified in this excerpt
findings.quote: The General Fund Capital Budget is substantial and is based on the best information available in terms of project costs. What is less certain but is in a far better position following the capital challenge sessions is the actual phasing of expenditure, which urgently needs further consideration and further prioritisation of any new projects particularly those still subject to a viable business case.

findings.headline: Greater Essex Unitary Authority set to launch April 2028 with funding already cut and mayoral election delayed until May 2028
findings.detail: Local government reorganisation poses financial and governance uncertainty. Mayoral elections have been delayed until May 2028, funding to those elections was reduced by two-thirds in the previous two years, and the new Unitary Authority for Greater Essex is due by April 2028. The S151 Officer states 'The risks have heightened' by these delays and cuts.
findings.matters: Council mergers create integration costs and transition uncertainty; this one is already experiencing funding reductions during the preparatory phase.
findings.figures: Mayoral election funding reduced by two-thirds in two years; unitary authority due April 2028
findings.quote: The financial implications arising from the Governments drive for Devolution and Local Government Reorganisation. The risks have heightened with the delay in Mayoral elections until May 2028 and funding reduced in the previous two financial years to those elections by two thirds. In addition, the impending decision by the Government on the Unitary Authority set up for Greater Essex, which is to be in place by April 2028.

findings.headline: Coastal infrastructure risks including cliff slips and pier remediation works acknowledged as unforeseen potential liabilities
findings.detail: Southend-on-Sea faces specific infrastructure risks related to its coastal location. The S151 Officer explicitly identifies 'the potential for cliff slips, pier remediation works, and any other unforeseen Council owned infrastructure issues' as exceptional risks that could call on reserves.
findings.matters: Coastal erosion and pier repair are location-specific liabilities that could create sudden, large capital calls outside normal budget cycles.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided; risks described as potential and unforeseen
findings.quote: The potential for cliff slips, pier remediation works, and any other unforeseen Council owned infrastructure issues.

findings.headline: Homelessness costs have increased significantly and require careful monitoring
findings.detail: The council explicitly flags 'recent significant increase in the cost of homelessness' as an exceptional risk requiring 'careful monitoring over the medium term to ensure the budgets are maintained and that all alternatives are being explored to reduce the cost of homelessness.'
findings.matters: Homelessness pressures are typically difficult to reverse and indicate demand-led spending that outpaces savings efforts.
findings.figures: Recent significant increase in homelessness costs, specific magnitude not quantified in this excerpt
findings.quote: The recent significant increase in the cost of homelessness which will need careful monitoring over the medium term to ensure the budgets are maintained and that all alternatives are being explored to reduce the cost of homelessness.

findings.headline: Waste and Street Cleansing is the largest single revenue contract with 'a lot of volatility' and implementation risks
findings.detail: The council's biggest single revenue contract is the waste disposal deal, which commenced with a new operational model in October 2025 (alternate weekly collection). The S151 Officer warns of 'a lot of volatility, new legislative and environmental requirements, which will potentially add additional risks and significant costs nationally across the market.' The council is 'working through the full implementation' but risks remain material.
findings.matters: The largest contract has acknowledged implementation uncertainty and external cost pressures; if it overruns, it directly threatens the council's financial plan.
findings.figures: Waste contract is described as 'the largest single revenue contract for the Council'; new model commenced October 2025
findings.quote: The Waste and Street Cleansing contract is the largest single revenue contract for the Council and has now fully commenced with a new operational and delivery model of alternate weekly recycling and waste collection from October 2025. The Council has mobilised the new waste collection and disposal arrangements and is now working through the full implementation to deliver operational excellence and value for money through effective contract management. There is a lot of volatility, new legislative and environmental requirements, which will potentially add additional risks and significant costs nationally across the market.

findings.headline: Children's and Adult Social Care facing major cost and demand increases with potential compulsory recovery plans
findings.detail: The S151 Officer explicitly identifies 'continuing major increasing cost, complexity and demand pressure trends for adult and children social care' as 'of particular and continuing growing concern.' The statement warns that the S151 Officer will 'insist on the development of robust and deliverable recovery plans' if these budgets are not demand-managed effectively, with specific mention of 'significant increases in the cost of children's residential care placements.'
findings.matters: Demand-led spending spirals in social care are difficult to arrest; forced recovery plans signal service delivery is exceeding budget headroom.
findings.figures: Social care noted as major increasing cost with significant increases specifically in children's residential care placements
findings.quote: The continuing major increasing cost, complexity and demand pressure trends for adult and children social care is of particular and continuing growing concern and it is important in both areas that the relevant Executive Director and management teams ensure these budgets are demand managed effectively to ensure the Council's future financial sustainability. If required I will insist on the development of robust and deliverable recovery plans to be put in place for these areas

findings.headline: Reserves increased to £12m to cover exceptional risks in social care, waste contract, and homelessness
findings.detail: The S151 Officer is raising unallocated General Fund reserves from £11m to £12m for 2026/27, specifically in response to acknowledged exceptional risks. These pressures have mainly focused in Children's Social Care but also include Adults Social Care, the new waste collection contract transition, and rising homelessness. The officer notes this is 'in response to the significant cost and demand pressures that have been experienced across Council services over several years now.'
findings.matters: A council that explicitly documents why it is increasing reserves signals material financial stress and acknowledges risks that could exhaust its safety net.
findings.figures: Reserves increasing from £11m to £12m; contingency set at £6.100m (1.22% of Council turnover of ~£0.5bn)
findings.quote: I am increasing the unallocated General Fund reserves level to £12 million, which will then be at my preferred level of reserves for 2026/27. This is in response to the significant cost and demand pressures that have been experienced across Council services over several years now. These pressures have mainly focussed within Children's Social Care but areas of increasing costs and demand are also prevalent within Adults Social Care, the transition to the new waste collection contract and rising homelessness concerns.

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 to Appendix 2 - Earmarked Reserves to 2030-31
findings.headline: Corporate reserves drop by 43% in a single year, from £16.1m to £9.1m, and stabilize at that lower level.
findings.detail: Corporate Reserves fall from £16,149k at 1/4/26 to £9,143k at 1/4/27 (a £7m reduction), then remain flat at £9,143k through 2030-31. This includes significant drawdowns of Business Initiatives Reserve (down to £1,017k), Service Redesign Reserve (down to £2,000k), and other transformation funds.
findings.matters: A sharp one-year reduction in general reserves used for corporate initiatives and service change signals that the council is consuming its strategic flexibility to deliver planned transformations; this matters to lenders assessing how much buffer remains for unforeseen costs.
findings.figures: Corporate Reserves: £16,149k (1/4/26) → £9,143k (1/4/27). Business Initiatives Reserve £2,281k → £1,017k; Service Redesign Reserve £3,599k → £2,000k

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 to Appendix 2 - Earmarked Reserves to 2030-31
findings.headline: Pension Reserve scheduled to be completely exhausted by April 2027.
findings.detail: Pension Reserve declines from £4,204k at 1/4/25 to £2,362k at 1/4/26, then is fully depleted (£0) by 1/4/27. This reserve is explicitly drawn down to zero and remains at zero through the rest of the forecast.
findings.matters: Complete depletion of a specific reserve earmarked for pensions creates a gap in that buffer; lenders need to understand why this reserve is being fully used and whether that indicates unmet pension liabilities or planned one-off costs.
findings.figures: Pension Reserve: £4,204k → £2,362k → £0k

findings.paper_title: Annex 2 to Appendix 2 - Earmarked Reserves to 2030-31
findings.headline: Total earmarked reserves forecast to fall by 34% over two years, from £59.4m to £39.4m by 2027.
findings.detail: General Fund earmarked reserves decline from £59,447k at 1/4/25 to £44,092k at 1/4/26, then to £39,385k at 1/4/27. They then remain flat through 2030-31. This represents a cumulative reduction of £20m in just two years.
findings.matters: A significant drawdown of financial reserves over a short period signals the council is relying on accumulated buffers to manage its position, reducing financial flexibility in the event of unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: Total General Fund Earmarked Reserves: £59,447k (1/4/25) → £44,092k (1/4/26) → £39,385k (1/4/27)
findings.quote: Total General Fund Earmarked Reserves 59,447...44,092...39,385

findings.headline: Outstanding PWLB debt of £339m growing to £343m; net new borrowing of £4m planned to continue capital investment program
findings.detail: General Fund PWLB borrowing is £267m with Housing Revenue Account debt of £72m, totaling £339m as of April 2026. The council plans £25m new borrowing in 2026/27 offset by £21m repayments, resulting in closing position of £343m. Essex County Council transferred debt of £8m is managed separately. The continued net borrowing in a high-rate environment indicates capital investment plans are proceeding despite elevated refinancing costs.
findings.matters: Tracks debt trajectory and total indebtedness; continued net borrowing in high-rate environment raises debt service costs and refinancing exposure
findings.figures: Opening PWLB debt GF £267m + HRA £72m = £339m; new loans £25m; repayments £21m; closing £343m; ECC transferred debt £8m to £7.7m
findings.quote: The funding available to support capital investment is based on an assumption that the Council will take out up to £25M of borrowing during 2026/27.

findings.headline: £21.9M of PWLB debt maturing in 2026/27, with £11.2M due September 2026 and £10.4M in March 2027, from 2001-2002 loans at 4.75%-5.5%
findings.detail: The council faces significant PWLB loan repayments in 2026/27 totaling £21.9m, with the largest maturities in September 2026 (£11.2m) and March 2027 (£10.4m). These were taken out in 2001 and 2002 at rates of 4.75% to 5.5%. Current PWLB rates range from 4.40% (1-year) to 5.94% (25-year), meaning refinancing will occur at materially higher rates than the original borrowing.
findings.matters: Significant maturity dates require refinancing management; refinancing at current PWLB rates will increase future debt service costs relative to original below-4% borrowing
findings.figures: £21.9M total repayments 2026/27, £11.2M (Sept 2026), £10.4M (March 2027), original rates 4.75%-5.5%, current PWLB rates 4.40%-5.94%
findings.quote: The next maturity dates of any PWLB debt redemption are: September 2026 for a sum of £11.2M (General Fund: £8.1m, Housing Revenue Account (HRA): £3.1m) and March 2027 for a sum of £10.4M (General Fund: £7.5m, Housing Revenue Account (HRA): £2.9m).

findings.headline: Council took no new PWLB loans in 2025/26 and plans to use internal cash flow instead of external borrowing in early 2026/27
findings.detail: Despite ongoing debt repayments, the council has not taken new PWLB loans in 2025/26. The strategy anticipates starting 2026/27 using temporary cash flow funds (internal borrowing) rather than external PWLB borrowing, with borrowing decisions deferred to later in the year as market conditions permit. The council maintains projected average cash balances of £112m (including £51.5m managed externally) to support this approach.
findings.matters: Shows disciplined debt cost management in response to high PWLB rates, but indicates dependence on maintaining large cash reserves to avoid expensive new borrowing
findings.figures: £112m average projected cash balances for 2026/27, £51.5m managed by external fund managers
findings.quote: So far in 2025/26 no new PWLB loans have been taken out. The Council is likely to begin 2026/27 in the second of the above scenarios.

findings.headline: General Fund capital expenditure forecast to drop to zero by 2030/31.
findings.detail: The council's planned General Fund capital investment declines sharply from £59.6m in 2026/27 to zero by 2030/31, with the steepest fall between 2026/27 and 2027/28. Housing Revenue Account capital also falls from £30.8m to £6.1m over the same period. The paper provides no explanation for this trajectory.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this reflects constrained finances, a deliberate debt repayment strategy, completion of major schemes, or merely forecasting uncertainty at the 4-5 year horizon. The cliff raises questions about service sustainability and investment priorities.

findings.headline: Council identifies material economic risks from pandemic effects and macro conditions that could further reduce income
findings.detail: The council acknowledges the pandemic will have long-term effects on the local economy and employment, and separately notes that rising government borrowing, inflation, interest rates, unemployment, failing businesses, and decreased consumption could reduce tax revenues and constrain public spending.
findings.matters: These risks could erode business rates and council tax income further, beyond the already-identified government funding reductions
findings.figures: Pre-pandemic: Southend attracted 7 million day visitors per year and 250,000 longer-stay visitors; approximately 66,200 people employed locally
findings.quote: There are likely to be additional pressures on Government spending in the medium to long term, because of increasing levels of borrowing and possible falling tax revenues due to risks around unemployment, failing businesses, decreased consumption, and significant shifts in the structure of the economy.

findings.headline: Aging population and deprivation are driving increased and more complex demand for services
findings.detail: The council identifies deprivation, aging population, and rising birth rates as structural drivers of increased service demand. This is expected to continue and will pressure budgets independently of funding changes.
findings.matters: Structural demand growth that outpaces funding creates unsustainable budget positions over the medium term
findings.figures: Southend is described as one of the most densely populated areas in the country
findings.quote: Deprivation, ageing population & rising birth rates leading to an increased demand for services

findings.headline: Acknowledged gap between capital investment ambitions and available resources will limit the number and value of viable schemes
findings.detail: The council identifies that it has major capital investment ambitions but recognizes it will not have resources to fund all schemes it would like to pursue. This means many capital projects will be deferred, cancelled, or unaffordable.
findings.matters: Constrained capital investment reduces asset maintenance and replacement, which can lead to deteriorating assets and higher future costs; it also signals limited financial headroom
findings.figures: No specific amounts
findings.quote: There will inevitably be a gap between the scale of our ambition and the level of available resources. This will limit the number and value of viable schemes that are affordable and deliverable.

findings.headline: Incremental efficiencies are insufficient; the council requires structural change in how services are designed and delivered
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that one-off savings and incremental efficiency programmes are not adequate to achieve long-term financial sustainability. It is committing to a comprehensive Transformation Strategy involving service redesign, operating model change, and demand management across ten organisation-wide themes.
findings.matters: A council that cannot achieve savings through normal efficiency measures and must resort to structural redesign faces execution risk and may struggle to deliver planned savings on schedule
findings.figures: No specific savings figures quantified
findings.quote: The scale and persistence of these pressures demonstrate that incremental efficiencies alone are insufficient. Long-term sustainability requires structural change in how services are designed and delivered, how residents access support, and how the Council manages resources.

findings.headline: Council is delivering an improvement plan following a Regulator for Social Housing judgement
findings.detail: The council acknowledges it has received a regulatory judgement from the Regulator for Social Housing and is now delivering an improvement plan in response. This indicates a governance or operational failure in the housing function, which is material for a council generating revenue from its housing stock.
findings.matters: Regulatory failure in social housing indicates governance weaknesses and potential operational or financial exposure in a major asset and income source
findings.figures: No details of the judgement or improvement costs provided
findings.quote: Emerging priorities include continued delivery of the improvement plan in response to the Regulator for Social Housing judgement and planning for the decarbonisation of the Council's housing stock

findings.headline: Central government funding has declined and is expected to continue declining throughout the strategy period
findings.detail: The council has experienced sustained reductions in core central government funding and identifies this as a significant challenge to its ambitions and service delivery. The document states this trend will continue for the foreseeable future and that funding sources are shifting from central grants to local (tax-based) income.
findings.matters: Structural funding decline without corresponding expenditure reduction creates persistent deficits and reduces debt capacity
findings.figures: No specific numbers for Southend's funding changes given
findings.quote: Like all Local Authorities, Southend-on-Sea City Council has seen a decline in the amount of funding it receives from central government grant. This represents a significant challenge to our ambitions and service delivery intentions.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Capital investment programme requires increased borrowing to be funded, with borrowing limits shown in prudential indicators.
findings.detail: The MTFS notes that an 'ambitious capital investment programme' is being partly funded by new borrowing, with PWLB rates assumed at 3.27-3.31% for General Fund and 3.88-4.03% for HRA over the period. Figure 28 (Borrowing Levels and Limits) shows the council's borrowing trajectory.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the council's borrowing decisions and debt serviceability, particularly given the structural deficit that requires transformation.
findings.figures: PWLB borrowing rates: General Fund 3.27-3.31%, HRA 3.88-4.03%; capital borrowing increasing to support investment programme
findings.quote: The ambitious capital investment programme, although partly funded by grants, other external contributions, capital receipts and revenue funding (such as Housing Revenue Account reserves), requires an increase in borrowing as set out in the Treasury Management and Capital Investment Strategies.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Council assumes more conservative council tax base growth (0.5% vs 1% government assumption) and collection rates (97.5% vs 100%), creating implicit income gaps.
findings.detail: The government's funding model assumes 1% annual council tax base growth and 100% collection, but Southend forecasts 0.5% base growth and 97.5% collection (though the council notes it benchmarks well on collection). These divergences create funding gaps where government forecasts assume more income than Southend actually expects to receive.
findings.matters: These assumptions affect the true scale of the budget gap. If Southend's conservative view is correct, the gap is larger than government funding implies; if optimistic, there is upside potential.
findings.figures: Council tax base growth: 0.5% vs 1% government assumption; collection rate: 97.5% vs 100% government assumption
findings.quote: A collection rate of 100% is unlikely, Southend-on-Sea City Council performs strongly and benchmarks favourably in terms of debt collection, but our ambitious collection rate target is set at 97.5% each year. It has been assumed that from 2027/28 the Council Tax base will increase by 0.5% per year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Waste management contract costs increased permanently by £4.4M annually following procurement, reflecting difficult market conditions for an essential service.
findings.detail: The council's waste management contract procurement concluded with an additional £4.4M per year added as a permanent increase to the 2025/26 base budget. This reflects rising service costs in an essential, discretionary-only-at-margin service.
findings.matters: This is a structural cost increase in a statutory service that cannot be delayed or avoided, and it reduces budget flexibility for other pressures.
findings.figures: £4.4M per year permanent increase to base revenue budget
findings.quote: After the conclusion of the procurement process an additional £4.4M per year was included in the Medium Term Financial Forecast and was included as a permanent increase in the 2025/26 base revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Looked After Children placements are highly volatile and create significant budget forecast uncertainty; a single additional residential placement costs £0.345M.
findings.detail: Sensitivity analysis shows that a single additional LAC residential placement increases the budget gap by £0.345M, and external foster care by £0.056M. The council explicitly acknowledges that individual placement decisions create forecast uncertainty in both the short and medium term, making budget forecasting difficult.
findings.matters: LAC numbers are outside council control (statutory duty) and can swing the financial position materially. This limits the reliability of medium-term forecasts.
findings.figures: +1 LAC residential placement = £0.345M budget impact; +1 LAC external foster care placement = £0.056M impact
findings.quote: The size of the impact of a single individual, particularly in the area of Looked After Children, is a significant challenge when it comes to short-term forecasting, even more so when we look to the medium-term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: National Living Wage costs for adult social care providers will escalate from £3.3M to £12.5M cumulatively over five years, an unavoidable structural cost pressure.
findings.detail: The budget assumes cumulative National Living Wage uplifts to social care providers of £3.3M in 2026/27, rising to £12.5M by 2030/31. This reflects government policy on minimum wage and the council's commitment to uplifting provider rates to maintain service sustainability.
findings.matters: This is a cost escalation entirely outside council control that will absorb a significant and growing share of budget headroom, reducing flexibility for other pressures.
findings.quote: National Living Wage (Adult Social Care Providers - Cumulative) [with values] £3.300M £5.600M £7.900M £10.200M £12.500M

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2030-31
findings.headline: Council has identified a structural deficit by 2030/31 requiring a transformation programme to bridge it.
findings.detail: The MTFS explicitly states that net cost reductions are required to bridge a medium-to-long-term deficit by 2030/31. The transformation programme includes zero-based budgeting reviews and activity analysis alongside existing projects (One Council redesign, Data Transformation, Estates, Children's Services Commissioning).
findings.matters: A council identifying a structural deficit and committing to a defined transformation programme is material financial planning information. Lenders need to assess whether the transformation can be delivered at pace.
findings.figures: Medium-to-long-term deficit by 2030/31; transformation programme scope includes zero-based budgeting and activity analysis
findings.quote: The overall level of net cost reduction required by Southend-on-Sea City Council to bridge a medium to long term deficit by 2030/31 requires a programme of work that not only supports the development of net cost reduction and transformation opportunities at a service level, but that also considers how these opportunities can be integrated into a renewed, sustainable, operating model.

findings.paper_title: App - PMG Auditors Annual Report for year ended 31-March-2025
findings.headline: Litigation and claims monitoring remains decentralised with no single authority view; prior-year audit recommendation still not implemented.
findings.detail: KPMG noted in the prior year that there is no centralised process for capturing and monitoring litigation/claims against the authority; these are managed by individual directorates. The recommendation remains ongoing into 2024/25. A new case management system was expected to address this but has not operated throughout the full year. This means potential themes or recurring issues may not be captured on a timely basis and contingent liabilities could be hidden.
findings.matters: Decentralised litigation tracking creates the risk of unknown or underquantified contingent liabilities that could materialise suddenly and affect covenant compliance or cash position.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: There is no consistent centralised process in place at the council for capturing and monitoring litigation and claims against the authority with these instead being managed by individual directorates on an 'as and when' basis... the implementation of the new case management system has not operated throughout 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: App - PMG Auditors Annual Report for year ended 31-March-2025
findings.headline: Usable reserves declined by £9.5m and cash position fell by £13.4m year-on-year.
findings.detail: Usable reserves fell from £192.570m in March 2024 to £183.028m in March 2025 (4.9% decline). Cash position fell from £32.265m to £18.865m (41.4% decline). General Fund reserve was replenished by £1m to reach £11m, masking the deterioration in overall reserve and liquidity position. The housing regulator applied C3 rating after year-end and children's services overspends are continuing into 2025/26.
findings.matters: A 41% decline in cash in a single year is material and concerning. Combined with recurring Children's Services overspends and the C3 housing rating, it suggests underlying structural cash pressures that reserves may be masking. Lenders track absolute and trend reserve/cash ratios as indicators of financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Usable reserves £183.028m (down from £192.570m), cash £18.865m (down from £32.265m), General Fund £11m (up from £10m)
findings.quote: Usable reserves of £183,028m as at 31 March 2025, down from £192,570m as at 31 March 2024... Year-end cash position 18.865m compared to 32.265m

findings.paper_title: App - PMG Auditors Annual Report for year ended 31-March-2025
findings.headline: Housing regulator issued C3 rating (serious failings) affecting 6,000 council-owned homes.
findings.detail: The Regulator for Social Housing undertook an inspection in April 2025 and issued a C3 judgement (issued 24 September 2025, after year-end but reported here) stating "serious failings in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards and significant improvement is needed." The Council had self-assessed as C2. KPMG assessed this as a significant governance risk but concluded the Council's improvement plan response was adequately robust and no formal weakness existed.
findings.matters: A C3 rating on 6,000 properties represents a material regulatory failure in a major asset base and revenue stream. It signals control deficiencies in landlord functions and potential compliance costs or statutory intervention if not resolved.
findings.figures: 6,000+ homes under council management, C3 rating (one step below C2 self-assessment)
findings.quote: During the financial year the Regulator for Social Housing has issued a regulatory judgement that there are serious failings in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards and significant improvement is needed.

findings.paper_title: App - PMG Auditors Annual Report for year ended 31-March-2025
findings.headline: Children's Services overspend is recurring and forecast to continue at £6.4m in 2025/26 despite mitigation efforts.
findings.detail: The Children, Young People and SEND directorate spent £6.1m over a £49.5m budget in 2024/25 (12.3% variance), down from £6.6m overspend in 2023/24. The driver is high-cost external residential and fostering placements due to national shortage of in-house capacity. KPMG identified this as a significant risk to financial sustainability. The Council has allocated permanent additional funding and a service line review has yielded £0.9m saving as at July 2026, but the Finance Performance Report still estimates £6.4m overspend for 2025/26 at period 4.
findings.matters: Demand-led overspends that persist across multiple years despite mitigation efforts signal either unrealistic budgeting, inadequate service redesign capacity, or structural cost growth the council cannot control. This is material to debt serviceability if the pattern continues.
findings.figures: £6.1m overspend 2024/25 (£49.5m budget), forecast £6.4m overspend 2025/26, improvement from £6.6m (20.3% of budget) in 2023/24 to £6.1m (12.3%) in 2024/25
findings.quote: The outturn showed a negative variance against budget of £6.1m. The Finance Performance Report July 2025 taken to September Cabinet estimates a continued overspend for the directorate of £6.4m, as at period 4 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget and Rent Setting Report 2026-2027 final
findings.headline: Tenant complaints volume has surged, requiring South Essex Homes to add complaints investigating capacity (2 staff, £79k)
findings.detail: Following significant national increases in tenant complaints (driven partly by Housing Ombudsman publicity), Southend has experienced a large local increase largely linked to repairs and maintenance contract performance. South Essex Homes is adding 2 complaints investigators (£79k) and an inspection and continuous improvement manager (£18k one-off) in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Rising complaint volumes reflect underlying service quality issues and resident dissatisfaction; increased staffing costs reduce operational efficiency and signal ongoing execution challenges
findings.figures: 2 additional complaints investigators at £79k in 2026/27; £18k one-off for inspection and improvement manager
findings.quote: There has been a significant increase nationally in the volume of complaints generated by tenants, partly due to increased advertising by the Housing Ombudsman. Locally we have also experienced a large increase, which have been largely linked to the performance of our current repairs and maintenance contract. Given the increase in volume there is a requirement to increase the number of complaints investigators...

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget and Rent Setting Report 2026-2027 final
findings.headline: HRA drawing £7.9M net from earmarked reserves to fund capital investment, reducing financial flexibility
findings.detail: Despite a £6.3M operating surplus, the HRA is appropriating £14.2M FROM the Capital Investment Reserve to fund the capital programme, resulting in a net £7.9M draw from earmarked reserves. General balances remain at £3.5M (above the £3M minimum), but the council is increasingly dependent on reserve depletion to fund capital ambitions.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdowns reduce financial flexibility and indicate capital investment exceeds annual operating cash generation; sustainability of this strategy depends on reserves not being exhausted
findings.figures: £6.275M operating surplus; £14.198M drawn from Capital Investment Reserve; £7.923M net appropriation from reserves; £3.5M general HRA balances (target £3M minimum)
findings.quote: Finally, to finance these ambitious plans it will also be necessary to appropriate £14,198,000 from the HRA Capital Investment Reserve. The net overall impact is an appropriation from earmarked reserves of £7,923,000 (£14,198,000 - £6,275,000) in 2026/27. General HRA balances will remain above the target of £3,000,000 at £3,500,000.

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget and Rent Setting Report 2026-2027 final
findings.headline: Awaab's Law (effective 27 October 2025) imposes statutory duty to investigate and fix damp and mould within prescribed timescales
findings.detail: New statutory requirement requiring social landlords to investigate and fix damp, mould and condensation within set timeframes. Compliance creates new service delivery obligations and cost implications for maintenance.
findings.matters: Statutory compliance obligation with regulatory enforcement risk; failure to meet timescales exposes the council to regulator action
findings.figures: Effective date 27 October 2025; prescribed timescales defined in the legislation
findings.quote: On 27 October 2025 Awaab's Law became effective which requires social landlords to investigate and fix damp, mould and condensation within prescribed timescales.

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget and Rent Setting Report 2026-2027 final
findings.headline: Repairs service failure triggered formal service improvement plan after surge in tenant complaints
findings.detail: Significant increase in tenant complaints about repairs and maintenance service performance led to a detailed Service Improvement Plan overseen by a joint council and South Essex Homes task group, indicating operational delivery issues with the new Axis Europe contract (from July 2024).
findings.matters: Service delivery failures indicate governance and execution risk; complaints signal resident dissatisfaction and potential revenue risk
findings.figures: New repairs contract from July 2024; service improvement plan implemented and ongoing management
findings.quote: There has been a requirement for significant management of the repairs and maintenance service after an increase in complaints from tenants about the service. As a result, a detailed Service Improvement Plan has been implemented and is being overseen by a joint Southend City Council and South Essex Homes task and finish group...

findings.paper_title: HRA Budget and Rent Setting Report 2026-2027 final
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing graded the council C3, requiring management improvement in Housing Consumer Standards
findings.detail: The council was inspected in April 2025 and graded C3 in September 2025. While 50% of inspected councils share this grade nationally, it indicates work needed on consumer standards. The council is developing a Provider Improvement Strategy and plans to pursue C2 regrading within a year.
findings.matters: Regulatory findings on consumer standards reflect management quality and compliance capability, which affect lender confidence
findings.figures: C3 grading; 50% of inspected councils grade C3 nationally; 6% grade C4; only 7 councils grade C1
findings.quote: We have been given a grading of C3, which means that we have work to do to improve some aspects of our work as a landlord.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account given C3 grading by Regulator of Social Housing, indicating service quality needs improvement despite strong financial position
findings.detail: In September 2025, the Regulator of Social Housing (RSH) graded the council's housing management C3, meaning aspects of work as a landlord need improving. The regulator's Consumer Standards assess the quality of landlord-tenant relationships. Despite already being aware of what needed improvement and making progress before publication, the council faces additional regulatory costs and requirements. The HRA is forecast to overspend by £0.704M in 2025/26 due to historical housing disrepair claims (£0.838M) and repairs contract overspend (£0.420M).
findings.matters: Low regulatory grading, even with strong headline financials, signals operational and reputational risk; unresolved housing disrepair claims and contract performance issues suggest assets may be deteriorating and tenant satisfaction eroding
findings.figures: C3 grading (aspects need improving), £0.704M HRA overspend, £0.838M historical housing disrepair claims, £0.420M repairs contract overspend
findings.quote: The Council has been given a grading of C3, meaning aspects of our work as a landlord need improving... Work is ongoing to continuously improve the services we provide to our housing tenants

findings.headline: Adult social care forecast overspend of £1.736M despite management action, with care package costs rising faster than inflation
findings.detail: Adult social care is forecast to overspend by £1.736M (down from £2.304M in P6, an improvement of £0.568M achieved through management reviews of existing care provision and securing health funding). However, older people's care packages are £1.636M overspent and mental health services are £2.107M overspent (up £0.291M from P6). The underlying driver is increasing complexity of cases requiring more hours of specialist support.
findings.matters: Persistent overspending in adult social care despite management action mirrors children's services pattern, suggesting a structural cost-of-care problem driven by acuity and market rates, not just demand volume
findings.figures: £1.736M overspend, older people care packages £1.636M overspent, mental health £2.107M overspent, improvement from P6 of £0.568M
findings.quote: Mental health is now reporting a forecast over spend of £2.107M, which is an increase of £0.291M since Period 6 (end of September 2025). This pressure and the increase costs continue to predominantly relate to care packages for those in supported living with more specialist support needs.

findings.headline: Capital programme budgets revised down from £94.8M to £64.8M within a single year, now requesting £21.228M of new amendments
findings.detail: The council approved a £94.8M capital programme in February 2025 but has revised it down to £64.8M through April, June, September and November changes. This report requests net amendments of £21.228M (including £2.818M for wheeled bins capitalisation under the new waste contract). The final revised programme is £218.534M over 5 years, but the council notes 51% is grant-funded and only 78% of external contributions had been received by November.
findings.matters: Repeated large revisions to the capital programme signal delivery constraints or reprioritization pressure; reliance on 51% grant funding creates vulnerability if external funding is delayed or clawed back, and unspent grants must be returned
findings.figures: Approved £94.8M, revised to £64.8M, amendments requested £21.228M, revised 5-year total £218.534M, 51% grant-funded, 78% of grants received by November
findings.quote: In February 2025 the Council agreed a capital investment programme budget for 2025/26 of £94.8M. The further changes agreed at April, June, September and November Cabinets have resulted in a revised budget for 2025/26 of £64.8M.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand up 19% year-on-year in November with £0.507M overspend despite £100M multi-year investment approved
findings.detail: Demand for temporary accommodation increased 19% in November 2025 compared to November 2024. The forecast overspend for 2025/26 is £0.507M. In July 2025, Cabinet approved in principle a £100M multi-year package to increase affordable housing and alleviate temporary accommodation pressure, but this requires profiling and multi-year planning, leaving immediate pressure unresolved.
findings.matters: Unchecked growth in temporary accommodation demand is expensive and destabilizing; the £100M investment is aspirational and unbudgeted, suggesting the council may lack capital headroom or revenue to fund its own stated solutions
findings.figures: 19% year-on-year increase November 2025 vs 2024, £0.507M forecast overspend, £100M multi-year investment package approved in principle
findings.quote: Demand for Temporary Accommodation (TA) continues to increase year on year... November 2025 saw a 19% increase in demand on the same period in 2024 for SCC

findings.headline: Savings delivery falling short with £0.250M and £0.057M of the £3.590M planned savings in Amber or Red status
findings.detail: Of the £3.590M of new savings and income initiatives approved in the 2025/26 budget, only 91% is on track to be achieved by year-end. While £3.283M is categorised as Green (will be achieved), £0.250M is Amber (will be partially achieved) and £0.057M is Red (unlikely to be achieved). Building control income is at risk (£0.180M shortfall), parks and open spaces have lost commercial contracts, and crematorium income is £0.600M short of target.
findings.matters: Shortfalls in approved savings plans indicate either weak pipeline design or operational barriers to delivery; 9% failure rate suggests further slippage is likely if demand pressures persist
findings.figures: £0.250M Amber, £0.057M Red out of £3.590M planned, building control shortfall £0.180M, crematorium income shortfall £0.600M
findings.quote: The following pie chart represents the value of savings which have been categorised as Green – will be achieved, Amber – will be partially achieved, Red – unlikely to be achieved

findings.headline: Direct Payments Support Service provider (Vibrance) failed on 20 November and entered administration 8 December, creating urgent continuity risk for 450 vulnerable adults and families
findings.detail: Vibrance was unable to safely continue payroll and managed account functions for 450 adults, children and families who directly employ Personal Assistants or rely on managed payments to agencies. The council took an emergency decision on 12 November to terminate the contract and implement continuity arrangements. The provider subsequently closed the service and went into administration. The council is still assessing the financial impact.
